screens.title: Self-Service Provisioning with AWS Service Catalog
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn why AWS Service Catalog exists and how it lets organizations balance developer speed with centralized governance. Think of Service Catalog as an internal app store for cloud infrastructure: administrators publish pre-approved products built from CloudFormation templates, and end users can launch those products without needing direct permissions to every underlying service. We will see how Products represent deployable units, how Portfolios group those products for specific teams, and how Constraints and launch roles enforce security and cost controls. A short concrete example: an administrator can publish a "Development Web Server" product defined by a CloudFormation template, restrict allowed instance sizes with a template constraint, and specify a launch role so developers can launch the server without needing EC2 permissions. You will also learn common mistakes to avoid, such as overly complex templates or overly permissive launch roles, and practical recommendations like testing in non-production. By the end of the chapter you will be able to explain the core components, sketch a safe provisioning workflow, and decide which constraints you need to meet governance objectives.

Module 4 › Chapter 4.7 › Overview
Self-Service Provisioning with AWS Service Catalog
Publish, control, and let teams launch approved infrastructure safely.
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
Concept snapshot
In this lesson
Products
Pre-approved templates
Portfolios
Grouping & access
Constraints
Governance rules
Coming up: administrator workflow, product design, constraints, and the end-user experience.
Why this matters
Self-service provisioning reduces wait times and shadow IT while ensuring resources are created according to security, cost, and tagging policies. Service Catalog centralizes approved configurations and enforces governance through constraints and controlled launch roles.
Internal app store metaphor
Imagine a catalog where developers choose a vetted product like a development web server. They supply a few parameters, and Service Catalog provisions the resources using an IAM launch role. This decouples who requests from who can create resources.
Explore Key Topics
Products & Templates
Products are defined by CloudFormation templates so instances are consistent and repeatable.
Portfolios & Access
Group products into portfolios to grant teams access to the right services.
Constraints & Launch Roles
Use template and launch constraints to enforce permitted parameters and use an IAM role for provisioning.
Start with a simple product in a non-production portfolio. Test template parameters and the launch role before rolling out to teams.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain what AWS Service Catalog is, identify its primary components, and configure governed products that teams can launch safely. You will describe how Products are built from CloudFormation templates and organized into Portfolios for access control. You will also learn to apply Constraints — both template constraints that limit parameter choices and launch constraints that assign an IAM role for provisioning — so governance and security are enforced at launch time. Finally, you will be able to guide an end-user through browsing and launching a provisioned product and monitor its status. Each objective includes a practical outcome: for example, you will analyze an example CloudFormation product template and decide which template constraint is needed to limit instance sizes. You will also practice designing a minimal launch role with only the permissions required to create the resources defined by a product. These skills reduce shadow IT, improve consistency, and keep cost and security controls intact.

screens.title: How we will practice
screens.narratorSegment: This chapter uses a guided lab walkthrough approach without requiring you to run every console step. You will conceptually navigate the administrator flow: create a CloudFormation-backed product, add it to a portfolio, configure template constraints to limit parameters, and define a launch constraint that uses an IAM role. You will also take the end-user perspective: browse the catalog, provide product parameters, and watch a provisioned product change status. Each practice step includes a checkpoint: for example, confirm that the product template creates consistent tags and that the launch role has minimum necessary permissions. We'll highlight common mistakes such as making templates too complex or assigning an overly permissive launch role. These practice steps will build judgment: when to keep a product minimal, how to choose which parameters to expose, and when to use constraints to enforce defaults. The goal is a repeatable checklist that helps you publish safe, easy-to-use products and maintain governance over time.

screens.title: What is AWS Service Catalog?
screens.narratorSegment: AWS Service Catalog is a managed service that lets organizations create and maintain catalogs of approved IT services. In practice this means administrators design a product once—typically as a CloudFormation template—that captures the exact resources, tags, and configuration the organization requires. End-users browse the catalog and launch provisioned products without needing direct permissions to each underlying service. A concrete example: an operations team packages a development web server as a product. The CloudFormation template includes an EC2 instance, a security group, and required tags. Developers simply select the product and supply a small set of parameters such as a key pair or environment name. This shortens delivery time and reduces inconsistent setups. A common misconception is that Service Catalog removes the need for IAM; it does not. Instead, it separates who requests a resource from who actually provisions it, via launch roles. Another pitfall is overloading the product template with too many parameters. Keep products focused so they are easy to maintain and secure. As you design a catalog, ask: does this product save time and reduce errors while keeping governance intact?

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.7 › What is Service Catalog?
Definition
AWS Service Catalog lets administrators publish approved IT services as products. End-users can then browse and launch these products without owning direct permissions to the underlying AWS resources.
Analogy
Think of it as an internal app store: products are apps, portfolios are shelves, and constraints are the store policies.
Concrete Example
A "Development Web Server" product that provisions an EC2 instance with required tags and a security group. Developers supply only safe parameters like key pair and environment name.
Key Takeaway

Service Catalog decouples who requests infrastructure from who actually provisions it, enabling governed self-service.

Misconceptions & Quick Checks
  • Service Catalog is not a permissions shortcut; it requires careful IAM in launch roles.
  • It does not replace CloudFormation; products are usually CloudFormation templates.
  • Avoid exposing every possible template parameter to users; keep the UX simple.
Why it matters
Faster provisioning for teams and consistent infrastructure reduce operational friction and improve compliance.

screens.title: Products: CloudFormation as the product definition
screens.narratorSegment: A Product in Service Catalog represents a deployable IT service and is typically defined by an AWS CloudFormation template. The template describes every resource the product needs, from compute and storage to networking and tags. Using CloudFormation ensures each instance of the product is provisioned identically, which is critical for security, monitoring, and cost allocation. For example, a product for a development web server might include an EC2 instance resource, a security group with specific inbound rules, and tags like environment and cost center. When administrators expose a limited set of parameters, end-users can still customize safe fields such as instance type or key pair while the template enforces defaults and required values. A frequent error is creating templates that are too complex or that expose too many parameters, which increases support overhead. The recommended approach is modular templates with clear outputs and a small, well-documented parameter surface. This makes it easier to apply template constraints later. To check your design, ask whether the template enforces tagging and whether it can be deployed repeatedly with predictable results. Products: CloudFormation as the product definition means define the product once in cloudformation to guarantee consistent resource creation and enforce organizational defaults.. In practical terms, how a product maps to a cloudformation template and why consistency matters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.7 › Products & Templates
Product structure
A product is normally the CloudFormation template plus metadata. It captures resources, parameters, tags, and outputs required for a consistent deployment.
Design checklist
  • Keep templates focused and modular to simplify maintenance.
  • Expose only safe parameters; prefer sensible defaults.
  • Enforce tagging for cost allocation and inventory management.
Concrete template example
Below is a simplified CloudFormation template example for a basic EC2-based product. Use this as a mental model for how a product translates to resources.
{
  "AWSTemplateFormatVersion": "2010-09-09",
  "Description": "Launches a basic EC2 instance for development.",
  "Parameters": {
    "InstanceType": { "Type": "String", "Default": "t2.micro", "AllowedValues": ["t2.micro","t2.small","t3.micro"] },
    "AMIId": { "Type": "AWS::EC2::Image::Id", "Default": "ami-0abcdef1234567890" },
    "KeyName": { "Type": "AWS::EC2::KeyPair::KeyName" }
  },
  "Resources": {
    "MyEC2Instance": {
      "Type": "AWS::EC2::Instance",
      "Properties": {
        "ImageId": { "Ref": "AMIId" },
        "InstanceType": { "Ref": "InstanceType" },
        "KeyName": { "Ref": "KeyName" },
        "Tags": [ { "Key": "Name", "Value": "ServiceCatalog-DevInstance" }, { "Key": "ManagedBy", "Value": "ServiceCatalog" } ]
      }
    }
  },
  "Outputs": { "InstanceId": { "Description": "The ID of the EC2 instance", "Value": { "Ref": "MyEC2Instance" } } }
}
Tip: Keep outputs clear so administrators can record essential identifiers and logs for the provisioned product.

screens.title: Portfolios vs Products
screens.narratorSegment: Products and portfolios are complementary concepts in Service Catalog. A product is the single deployable unit, usually represented by a CloudFormation template. A portfolio is a collection of products that you present to a team, department, or role. Portfolios are the access control layer: you grant users or IAM principals access to a portfolio, not to individual resources inside a product. For instance, you might create a "Developer Portfolio" containing development-grade products and a separate "Production Portfolio" with hardened products. This separation allows you to grant a developer permission to launch development products without giving them the ability to provision production infrastructure. A common mistake is assigning product-level permissions directly to many users; instead, use portfolios to centralize access management. Another advantage is segregation by environment or cost center, which simplifies reporting. When deciding how to group products, consider user roles, compliance boundaries, and lifecycle; portfolios should reflect who needs access and why. Portfolios vs Products means assign portfolios to teams so they see only approved products and never direct resource permissions.. In practical terms, how products and portfolios relate and how to use them for access control. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.7 › Portfolios vs Products
Product (single unit)
Represents one deployable service defined by a CloudFormation template, with parameters and outputs. Examples: development web server, managed database instance.
Characteristics
  • Template-backed, repeatable provisioning
  • Has parameters, tags, and outputs
  • Designed for consistency
Portfolio (collection)
A container of products used to grant sets of users access to approved services. Use portfolios to separate environments and roles, and to simplify permission management.
When to use portfolios
Group by team, environment, or compliance need so users see only the products appropriate for them.
Example: Developer Portfolio
Contains development server and test database products with relaxed cost limits.
Example: Production Portfolio
Contains hardened products and strict template constraints to enforce sizes and encryption.
Quick Tip
Prefer fewer portfolios focused on clear boundaries rather than many overlapping ones.

screens.title: Template Constraints
screens.narratorSegment: Template constraints let administrators modify or restrict the parameters allowed at product launch, providing a straightforward governance mechanism. For instance, if a CloudFormation template allows many EC2 instance types, a template constraint can limit the choices to a safe subset like t2. micro and t3. micro to control cost. Template constraints do not modify the fundamental template logic; they restrict what an end-user can select at launch. A concrete example: your product template defines InstanceType with several allowed values, but an administrator applies a template constraint that narrows allowed values to approved sizes for the given portfolio. A common misconception is that template constraints fully rewrite templates — they do not. They act as an overlay at launch time. When designing constraints, think about which parameters affect cost, compliance, or security and restrict those first. Always test constraints in a non-production portfolio to confirm the user experience and to avoid unexpected launch failures. Template Constraints means use them to limit choices that influence cost or security without changing the underlying template.. In practical terms, how template constraints limit parameter choices to enforce governance. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.7 › Template Constraints
Process: Applying a template constraint
  1. Identify parameters that affect cost, security, or compliance, such as instance type, storage size, or encryption options.
  2. Create a template constraint that narrows AllowedValues or enforces defaults for those parameters.
  3. Attach the constraint to a product within a portfolio and test launches in a non-production portfolio.
  4. Monitor launches for validation errors and adjust the constraint if legitimate use cases are blocked.
Misconception check: constraints don’t replace careful template design — they complement templates by enforcing organization policies at launch time.
Example
If a template allows instance types m5.large, m5.xlarge, and m5.2xlarge, a template constraint can restrict allowed values to m5.large only for a specific portfolio to control cost.
Key Takeaway

Template constraints are an overlay to limit user choices for safer, cheaper launches.

screens.title: Launch Constraints and IAM Roles
screens.narratorSegment: A launch constraint specifies an IAM role that Service Catalog assumes when creating the resources defined by a product. This is a powerful security pattern because end-users need only permission to launch the product itself, not permission to create the underlying resources directly. The launch role contains the actual permissions required to provision resources such as ec2:RunInstances or rds:CreateDBInstance. For example, developers may lack ec2:RunInstances but can launch a product; Service Catalog uses the launch role with the proper permissions to provision the EC2 instance on their behalf. A common mistake is granting the launch role broader permissions than required, which undermines governance. Follow least privilege — grant only the actions necessary to create the resources defined in the template. Another practical point is to test the launch role in a sandbox portfolio to verify it can create resources and attach required tags. The separation provided by launch constraints simplifies auditing and helps ensure that users cannot escalate their permissions by launching products. Launch Constraints and IAM Roles means service catalog assumes the launch role to create resources, keeping end-user permissions minimal and centralized.. In practical terms, how launch constraints separate user permissions from provisioning permissions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.7 › Launch Constraints
What a launch constraint does
When a product is launched, Service Catalog assumes the specified IAM role and uses its permissions to create resources. End-users need only permission to launch the product itself.
Best practices
  • Grant the launch role only the permissions necessary to provision resources declared in the template.
  • Test the role in non-production to ensure no missing permissions or excess privileges.
  • Use tagging and IAM condition keys to limit resource scope where possible.
Illustrative scenario
Developers can launch a web server product. They do not need ec2:RunInstances. Service Catalog assumes a launch role that has ec2:RunInstances and necessary tagging permissions to provision the instance on their behalf.
Misconception check: granting end-users product launch permissions does not give them underlying resource privileges when a proper launch role is used.

screens.title: Example Product Template
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a simplified CloudFormation template that would back a Service Catalog product. The template declares parameters for InstanceType, AMIId, and KeyName so an administrator can control what can be changed at launch. Resources include the EC2 instance with explicit tags that help with cost allocation and inventory. Outputs, such as the InstanceId, help administrators capture identifiers after provisioning. When reviewing a template for Service Catalog, verify that required tags are present, that parameters have sensible defaults, and that AllowedValues are explicit where necessary. Remember that template constraints can further restrict parameter choices at launch time, so the template does not need to be the only control point. A common oversight is leaving too many open parameters or relying solely on naming conventions; include tags and outputs that make automated inventory and billing easier. Finally, always test the template by launching it through Service Catalog in a sandbox portfolio to ensure the launch role can create the resources and that outputs appear as expected. Simplified CloudFormation template (example)
{
  "AWSTemplateFormatVersion": "2010-09-09",
  "Description": "Launches a basic EC2 instance for development.",
  "Parameters": {
    "InstanceType": { "Type": "String", "Default": "t2.micro", "AllowedValues": ["t2.micro","t2.small","t3.micro"] },
    "AMIId": { "Type": "AWS::EC2::Image::Id", "Default": "ami-0abcdef1234567890" },
    "KeyName": { "Type": "AWS::EC2::KeyPair::KeyName" }
  },
  "Resources": {
    "MyEC2Instance": {
      "Type": "AWS::EC2::Instance",
      "Properties": {
        "ImageId": { "Ref": "AMIId" },
        "InstanceType": { "Ref": "InstanceType" },
        "KeyName": { "Ref": "KeyName" },
        "Tags": [ { "Key": "Name", "Value": "ServiceCatalog-DevInstance" }, { "Key": "ManagedBy", "Value": "ServiceCatalog" } ]
      }
    }
  },
  "Outputs": { "InstanceId": { "Description": "The ID of the EC2 instance", "Value": { "Ref": "MyEC2Instance" } } }
}
Review checklist
  • Do parameters have safe defaults and limited AllowedValues?
  • Are required tags included for billing and inventory?
  • Are outputs defined for key identifiers administrators need?
Misconception check: templates should not expose every internal option — hide complexity and expose only what the end-user needs to provide.

screens.title: End-User Launch Experience (Conceptual)
screens.narratorSegment: From an end-user perspective, Service Catalog is a simple provisioning interface. Users browse portfolios shared with them and see cataloged products. When launching a product they typically supply a few parameters defined by the template, such as key pair, environment name, or approved instance type. If a template constraint is attached, the available options at launch may be narrower than what the template originally allowed; this enforces policy without requiring user awareness of underlying governance. After initiating a launch, the user sees a provisioned product in their console with a status like Available, Under Change, or Error. If the launch role lacks permissions or a constraint blocks a choice, the launch returns an error status which administrators can inspect. A useful mental model is that the end-user interacts with a curated menu, while administrators control the kitchen: users choose what they need, and administrators ensure the cooking follows the recipe and rules. Encourage teams to test launches in a sandbox portfolio so that launch paths and constraint effects are clear before broad rollout. Module 4 › Chapter 4.7 › End-User Flow
Launch steps (conceptual)
  1. Browse portfolios shared with your account to find the desired product.
  2. Select the product and enter only the allowed parameters, such as key pair or environment name.
  3. Submit the launch request; Service Catalog assumes the launch role to provision resources.
  4. Monitor the provisioned product status and troubleshoot with operations if an error appears.
Status & troubleshooting
Provisioned products show statuses like Available, Under Change, or Error. If a launch fails, check template constraints, launch role permissions, and CloudFormation error messages. Administrators should provide clear logs and contact points.
Pro Tip

Provide concise product documentation so end-users know which parameters to supply and what the expected outputs are.

screens.title: Provisioned Product Lifecycle
screens.narratorSegment: Provisioned products are instances of a product launched by an end-user. Their lifecycle starts when a user requests a launch and ends when the resources are terminated. Typical statuses include Available when provisioning completes successfully, Under Change when updates or updates in progress are applied, and Error when provisioning fails. When troubleshooting an Error status, administrators should inspect the CloudFormation events that underlie the product, check that the launch role has required permissions, and ensure template constraints did not block a parameter value. Updates to a provisioned product can be performed through Service Catalog, which triggers corresponding CloudFormation updates. A misconception is assuming a provisioned product is immutable; you can change parameters or update the product through controlled change processes, but do so carefully to avoid drift. Regularly review provisioned products for tagging compliance and resource drift. This lifecycle perspective helps operations plan monitoring, backups, and decommissioning policies aligned with governance goals. Provisioned Product Lifecycle means monitor status changes, use cloudformation events for troubleshooting, and manage updates through controlled change workflows.. In practical terms, track status, updates, and common error modes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. screens.title: Common Pitfalls and Best Practices
screens.narratorSegment: There are several recurring pitfalls when implementing Service Catalog that you should proactively avoid. First, overly complex CloudFormation templates with many parameters increase cognitive load and make maintenance costly. Keep templates modular and expose only the parameters end-users must change. Second, granting overly permissive launch roles undermines governance — always follow least privilege by granting only the actions necessary to create the resources declared in the template. Third, skipping testing in a non-production portfolio can let errors slip into production. Always validate launch paths, template constraints, and the launch role in a sandbox. Best practices include applying template constraints to parameters that affect cost or compliance, requiring tags for billing and reporting, and regularly reviewing portfolios to remove stale products. Also document each product with expected parameters and outputs so end-users and operators can understand what the product provisions. These habits keep the catalog manageable and aligned with organizational policies over time. Module 4 › Chapter 4.7 › Best Practices
Keep templates simple
Modular templates are easier to maintain and test. Avoid exposing unnecessary parameters to users.
Least privilege launch roles
Grant only required permissions to the launch role. Excess privileges defeat the purpose of centralized provisioning.
Test in non-production
Validate constraints and roles in a sandbox portfolio before broad rollout.
Document each product
Provide concise instructions on expected parameters, outputs, and troubleshooting steps.
Enforce tagging
Include required tags in templates to support cost allocation and inventory tracking.
Regular reviews
Periodically review portfolios and remove stale or irrelevant products.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn why AWS Service Catalog exists and how it lets organizations balance developer speed with centralized governance. Think of Service Catalog as an internal app store for cloud infrastructure: administrators publish pre-approved products built from CloudFormation templates, and end users can launch those products without needing direct permissions to every underlying service. We will see how Products represent deployable units, how Portfolios group those products for specific teams, and how Constraints and launch roles enforce security and cost controls. A short concrete example: an administrator can publish a "Development Web Server" product defined by a CloudFormation template, restrict allowed instance sizes with a template constraint, and specify a launch role so developers can launch the server without needing EC2 permissions. You will also learn common mistakes to avoid, such as overly complex templates or overly permissive launch roles, and practical recommendations like testing in non-production. By the end of the chapter you will be able to explain the core components, sketch a safe provisioning workflow, and decide which constraints you need to meet governance objectives.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain what AWS Service Catalog is, identify its primary components, and configure governed products that teams can launch safely. You will describe how Products are built from CloudFormation templates and organized into Portfolios for access control. You will also learn to apply Constraints — both template constraints that limit parameter choices and launch constraints that assign an IAM role for provisioning — so governance and security are enforced at launch time. Finally, you will be able to guide an end-user through browsing and launching a provisioned product and monitor its status. Each objective includes a practical outcome: for example, you will analyze an example CloudFormation product template and decide which template constraint is needed to limit instance sizes. You will also practice designing a minimal launch role with only the permissions required to create the resources defined by a product. These skills reduce shadow IT, improve consistency, and keep cost and security controls intact.

This chapter uses a guided lab walkthrough approach without requiring you to run every console step. You will conceptually navigate the administrator flow: create a CloudFormation-backed product, add it to a portfolio, configure template constraints to limit parameters, and define a launch constraint that uses an IAM role. You will also take the end-user perspective: browse the catalog, provide product parameters, and watch a provisioned product change status. Each practice step includes a checkpoint: for example, confirm that the product template creates consistent tags and that the launch role has minimum necessary permissions. We'll highlight common mistakes such as making templates too complex or assigning an overly permissive launch role. These practice steps will build judgment: when to keep a product minimal, how to choose which parameters to expose, and when to use constraints to enforce defaults. The goal is a repeatable checklist that helps you publish safe, easy-to-use products and maintain governance over time.

AWS Service Catalog is a managed service that lets organizations create and maintain catalogs of approved IT services. In practice this means administrators design a product once—typically as a CloudFormation template—that captures the exact resources, tags, and configuration the organization requires. End-users browse the catalog and launch provisioned products without needing direct permissions to each underlying service. A concrete example: an operations team packages a development web server as a product. The CloudFormation template includes an EC2 instance, a security group, and required tags. Developers simply select the product and supply a small set of parameters such as a key pair or environment name. This shortens delivery time and reduces inconsistent setups. A common misconception is that Service Catalog removes the need for IAM; it does not. Instead, it separates who requests a resource from who actually provisions it, via launch roles. Another pitfall is overloading the product template with too many parameters. Keep products focused so they are easy to maintain and secure. As you design a catalog, ask: does this product save time and reduce errors while keeping governance intact?

A Product in Service Catalog represents a deployable IT service and is typically defined by an AWS CloudFormation template. The template describes every resource the product needs, from compute and storage to networking and tags. Using CloudFormation ensures each instance of the product is provisioned identically, which is critical for security, monitoring, and cost allocation. For example, a product for a development web server might include an EC2 instance resource, a security group with specific inbound rules, and tags like environment and cost center. When administrators expose a limited set of parameters, end-users can still customize safe fields such as instance type or key pair while the template enforces defaults and required values. A frequent error is creating templates that are too complex or that expose too many parameters, which increases support overhead. The recommended approach is modular templates with clear outputs and a small, well-documented parameter surface. This makes it easier to apply template constraints later. To check your design, ask whether the template enforces tagging and whether it can be deployed repeatedly with predictable results. Products: CloudFormation as the product definition means define the product once in cloudformation to guarantee consistent resource creation and enforce organizational defaults.. In practical terms, how a product maps to a cloudformation template and why consistency matters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Products and portfolios are complementary concepts in Service Catalog. A product is the single deployable unit, usually represented by a CloudFormation template. A portfolio is a collection of products that you present to a team, department, or role. Portfolios are the access control layer: you grant users or IAM principals access to a portfolio, not to individual resources inside a product. For instance, you might create a "Developer Portfolio" containing development-grade products and a separate "Production Portfolio" with hardened products. This separation allows you to grant a developer permission to launch development products without giving them the ability to provision production infrastructure. A common mistake is assigning product-level permissions directly to many users; instead, use portfolios to centralize access management. Another advantage is segregation by environment or cost center, which simplifies reporting. When deciding how to group products, consider user roles, compliance boundaries, and lifecycle; portfolios should reflect who needs access and why. Portfolios vs Products means assign portfolios to teams so they see only approved products and never direct resource permissions.. In practical terms, how products and portfolios relate and how to use them for access control. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Template constraints let administrators modify or restrict the parameters allowed at product launch, providing a straightforward governance mechanism. For instance, if a CloudFormation template allows many EC2 instance types, a template constraint can limit the choices to a safe subset like t2. micro and t3. micro to control cost. Template constraints do not modify the fundamental template logic; they restrict what an end-user can select at launch. A concrete example: your product template defines InstanceType with several allowed values, but an administrator applies a template constraint that narrows allowed values to approved sizes for the given portfolio. A common misconception is that template constraints fully rewrite templates — they do not. They act as an overlay at launch time. When designing constraints, think about which parameters affect cost, compliance, or security and restrict those first. Always test constraints in a non-production portfolio to confirm the user experience and to avoid unexpected launch failures. Template Constraints means use them to limit choices that influence cost or security without changing the underlying template.. In practical terms, how template constraints limit parameter choices to enforce governance. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A launch constraint specifies an IAM role that Service Catalog assumes when creating the resources defined by a product. This is a powerful security pattern because end-users need only permission to launch the product itself, not permission to create the underlying resources directly. The launch role contains the actual permissions required to provision resources such as ec2:RunInstances or rds:CreateDBInstance. For example, developers may lack ec2:RunInstances but can launch a product; Service Catalog uses the launch role with the proper permissions to provision the EC2 instance on their behalf. A common mistake is granting the launch role broader permissions than required, which undermines governance. Follow least privilege — grant only the actions necessary to create the resources defined in the template. Another practical point is to test the launch role in a sandbox portfolio to verify it can create resources and attach required tags. The separation provided by launch constraints simplifies auditing and helps ensure that users cannot escalate their permissions by launching products. In practical terms, how launch constraints separate user permissions from provisioning permissions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Provisioned products are instances of a product launched by an end-user. Their lifecycle starts when a user requests a launch and ends when the resources are terminated. Typical statuses include Available when provisioning completes successfully, Under Change when updates or updates in progress are applied, and Error when provisioning fails. When troubleshooting an Error status, administrators should inspect the CloudFormation events that underlie the product, check that the launch role has required permissions, and ensure template constraints did not block a parameter value. Updates to a provisioned product can be performed through Service Catalog, which triggers corresponding CloudFormation updates. A misconception is assuming a provisioned product is immutable; you can change parameters or update the product through controlled change processes, but do so carefully to avoid drift. Regularly review provisioned products for tagging compliance and resource drift. This lifecycle perspective helps operations plan monitoring, backups, and decommissioning policies aligned with governance goals. There are several recurring pitfalls when implementing Service Catalog that you should proactively avoid. First, overly complex CloudFormation templates with many parameters increase cognitive load and make maintenance costly. Keep templates modular and expose only the parameters end-users must change. Second, granting overly permissive launch roles undermines governance — always follow least privilege by granting only the actions necessary to create the resources declared in the template. Third, skipping testing in a non-production portfolio can let errors slip into production. Always validate launch paths, template constraints, and the launch role in a sandbox. Best practices include applying template constraints to parameters that affect cost or compliance, requiring tags for billing and reporting, and regularly reviewing portfolios to remove stale products. Also document each product with expected parameters and outputs so end-users and operators can understand what the product provisions. These habits keep the catalog manageable and aligned with organizational policies over time. This conceptual activity walks you through the end-user experience without requiring a live console. Start by imagining you sign in and open the Service Catalog dashboard as an end-user. You find the Developer Portfolio and see products like "Development Web Server." You select the product and click to launch. You provide parameters such as InstanceType set to t2. micro, KeyName set to your key pair, and Environment set to Dev. If a template constraint restricts instance types, your available choices will reflect that restriction. When you submit the launch, Service Catalog assumes the launch role and begins provisioning via CloudFormation. Back in the console you see a new provisioned product entry with a status. If the status becomes Error, check whether a parameter was blocked by a template constraint or whether the launch role lacked a specific permission. If everything succeeds, the product becomes Available and the console shows outputs such as the InstanceId. Reflect: how would this flow change if you were a production operator versus a developer, and what constraints would you expect to be stricter in production?

Here are three essential concepts to hold onto as you design a Service Catalog. First, AWS Service Catalog itself: a managed service that lets organizations publish and manage catalogs of approved IT services so teams can self-provision without bypassing governance. Second, a Product: a deployable unit defined by a CloudFormation template that ensures every deployment is consistent and includes required tags and outputs. Third, a Portfolio: a collection of products that you grant to teams or roles, which simplifies access control and environment separation. Keep these definitions front-of-mind when you design catalogs: they determine who sees what and how provisioning respects your policies. Finish by remembering three operational concepts that determine how governance is enforced. First, Constraint: a general rule that governs how a product is deployed, implemented as template or launch constraints. Second, Template Constraint: an overlay that restricts parameter choices at launch time, useful to limit instance types or storage sizes. Third, Launch Constraint: the specification of an IAM role that Service Catalog assumes to provision resources, separating user launch permissions from provisioning permissions. These concepts let you create a predictable provisioning model: templates define the recipe, constraints shape the ingredients, and the launch role does the cooking with appropriate permissions. As a reflective question, consider which parameters in your current templates should be locked down with template constraints and which actions the launch role must be allowed to perform.
